## Paper

## Abstract

Classical and quantum bits serve as cornerstone in information science. As this field rapidly evolves, the interplay between the two continues to enrich and inspire each other. Here, analog superposition states and analog nonseparable states are theoretically explored and experimentally demonstrated in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. To implement the quantum-inspired states in classical system, we have developed a reconfigurable metasurface capable of synthesizing analog superposition states across the temporal dimension and analog nonseparable states across spatial and polarization dimensions. Due to its unique features of analog superposition and non-separability, the proposed metasurface holds great potential to revolutionize the information processing capabilities beyond those offered by the classical information metasurface. This work not only offers a reconfigurable physical platform to advance classical and quantum information, but also will both enable unknown wave phenomena and provide promising perspectives in the fields of information science, quantum physics and material science.

---

## Introduction

In recent years, the rapid advancement of quantum mechanics1–3 has attracted increasing attention to the field of quantum information science4–6. As an interdisciplinary discipline bridging quantum physics and information science, quantum information science is transforming research paradigms in both science and technology with its substantial practical potential and unique capabilities. Specifically, quantum communication7–10 leverages the phenomenon of quantum entanglement to ensure the security of information communication, whereas quantum computation11–14 exploits the principle of quantum superposition to achieve computational power that surpasses that of classical computers, thereby driving transformative advances in fields of materials science, chemistry, and beyond. Furthermore, the recent progress in quantum sensing15–18 and measurement19–21 technologies has significantly improved the performance of traditional sensors and measurement systems to unprecedented levels.

The success of quantum information science has not only stimulated the flourishing of quantum optics22,23, but has also propelled the development of quantum metasurfaces24–27. Metasurfaces are planar artificial structures composed of subwavelength meta-atoms arranged in either periodic or aperiodic configurations28–32. However, most passive metasurfaces lack the capability to reconfigure their electromagnetic (EM) functionality once fabricated33,34, which significantly limits their practical applications. To address this challenge, the concept of reconfigurable metasurfaces35–38 has been introduced. The switching capabilities of the EM response in reconfigurable metasurfaces have motivated the development of the digital metasurfaces39 and subsequently evolved into information metasurfaces40–48, which serve to bridge information science and classical EM physics.

The basic information-processing units of information metasurfaces are based on classical digital bits, which offer benefits such as stability, ease of storage and transmission, and operational simplicity. However, they suffer from limitations in information capacity and parallel-processing capability. In contrast, quantum bits (qubits)49–51 exhibit unprecedented superiority in these aspects, offering potential solutions to address the challenges currently faced by classical digital bits. However, qubits are often unstable, difficult to store and transmit, and highly susceptible to environmental interference. To combine the respective advantages of classical bits and qubits, several attempts are being made to develop quantum-inspired bits52,53 in classical systems. Nevertheless, current studies are mostly limited to theoretical explorations, and the experimental realization and manipulation of quantum-inspired states in classical systems remain a significant challenge in this field.

In this work, we investigate the quantum-inspired states of reconfigurable metasurfaces to emulate the mathematical and geometrical representations of the quantum states. We should clarify that the quantum-inspired states discussed here are implemented in a classical system rather than in a quantum system. Generally, the mathematical representation provides a theoretical framework to rigorously describe the quantum-inspired states, whereas the geometric representation offers an intuitive way to understand them. Specifically, we initiate our discussions by introducing the concept and mathematical framework of the analog superposition state to explore the analog superposition behavior of the EM waves based on a reconfigurable metasurface in a classical system. To validate the correctness of our theoretical model, we perform numerical simulations on the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. All numerical simulations were conducted based on the fundamental frequency, without considering the influence of other harmonic frequencies. Each meta-atom on the metasurface can be individually controlled through mechanical rotation, thereby enabling flexible manipulation of the polarization state on the Poincaré sphere. Notably, the reconfigurable feature of the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface allows it to transform the polarization state by reaching all possible points on the Poincaré sphere, which is a crucial ability to implement the analog superposition state. We further demonstrate an analog nonseparable state that mirrors the entanglement between light spin and far-field spatial modes. In a proof-of-concept experiment, we show excellent agreement between the experimental results and numerical simulations, thus affirming that the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is a feasible platform to realize the concept of quantum-inspired states. We believe that the introduction of the quantum-inspired bit and the realization of the reconfigurable array platform will advance the developments in various fields, including quantum physics, information science, and metamaterials.

---

## Results

Reconfigurable time-varying metasurface
We commence our analysis by investigating the EM properties of various meta-atoms to explore the correlations among different information bit types. In classical information processing, a classical bit is generally represented by the binary state 0 or 1. Physically, these classical bits are inherently binary systems, distinguished by their exclusive occupation of one of two possible states. The EM properties of the meta-atom in the classical information metasurfaces are controlled by a binary state, namely the coding state 0 (ON) or 1 (OFF), by switching the PIN diode, as depicted in Fig. 1a. Mathematically, the binary state can be formulated as |Ψ〉=(1−δ)|0〉+δ|1〉, where |0〉 and |1〉 denote the respective reflection polarization states (i.e., |Ψ〉) of the meta-atom when the PIN diode is in its ON (δ=0) and OFF (δ=1) configurations, with δ being restricted to 0 or 1. It is noteworthy that the operations involving the classical bits are deterministic, complying with Boolean algebra principles. In the classical context, the classical bits are limited to process a single state at any given moment. In contrast, the quantum bits leverage the superposition property to provide significant advantages in parallel information processing. Generally, the Bloch sphere is used as a geometric representation to succinctly and clearly convey this concept, as depicted in Fig. 1b. In this representation, the state of a quantum bit can be visualized at any location on the Bloch sphere, transcending the limitations of classical information processing.

The mathematical representation of a quantum bit can be expressed as a linear superposition of two polarization states, namely |Ψ〉=α|0〉+β|1〉. The coefficients, α and β, are complex numbers that are subjected to normalization and probabilistic constraints |α|2+|β|2=1. After initializing the global phase to zero and defining the relative phase as ϕ, the state |Ψ〉 has only two degrees of freedom. The Bloch sphere surface, which represents the qubit state space, is inherently two-dimensional, providing two distinct local degrees of freedom. As a result, this state can be mathematically represented by |Ψi= cosθ|0i+eiϕ sinθ|1i. In this context, the polar angle θ (ranging from 0 to π) and the azimuthal angle ϕ (from 0 to 2π) correspondingly denote the quantum bit’s position on the Bloch sphere, akin to the latitude and longitude. With the determination of θ and ϕ, the quantum state is fully defined and can be geometrically represented.

Inspired by the mathematical and geometric representations of quantum bits, here we introduce a concept of quantum-inspired bits (as shown in Fig. 1b), the state of which can be mathematically expressed as an analog superposition state:
|Ψi= cosθ|Ri+eiϕ sinθ|Li. Here, |R〉 and |L〉 represent two orthogonal bases that constitute the bit: right-handed circular polarization (RCP) and left-handed circular polarization (LCP) states. This mathematical representation is applicable to the RCP plane-wave incidence scenarios. For the LCP incidence, the coefficients associated with two orthogonal bases should be interchanged.

To implement the aforementioned analog superposition state, we propose a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface as a feasible physical platform. Additionally, the metasurface exhibits analog nonseparable state properties, as shown in Fig. 1c. Different from the conventional digital coding metasurface, the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface employs a discrete periodic configuration of meta-atoms, which are designed to overcome the rotation-related challenges, including friction and collisions between adjacent meta-atoms. We employ a multi-layered metal-insulator-metal spacer structure to design the meta-atom, optimizing their performance, and integrate stepping motors for actuation (details can be found in the “Methods” section), as illustrated in Fig. 1d. This structure facilitates the flexible control of the reflected wave’s polarization state over the Poincaré sphere through both forward and backward stepping and rotational stepping dimensions in practice. Given that the analog superposition state corresponds to the polarization state of the reflected wave, we opt to represent this using the Poincaré sphere rather than the Bloch sphere, as shown in Fig. 1b for more accurate visualization. We note that the realization of this concept essentially relies on the introduction of a temporal dimension and rotational transformations in the same reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom. In quantum physics, a qubit has an instant superposition of states. In our case, the analog superposition of states is implemented in a certain time interval on the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom by manipulating its rotation angle at different times. It is important to emphasize that both the time interval and the system’s response time remain on the order of milliseconds. In principle, minimizing the time interval towards zero would yield an analog of the qubit superposition state. More details of the theoretical derivations for the mathematical and geometric representations of the analog superposition state in reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces can be found in the Supplementary Note 1.

Reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom
The configuration of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is illustrated in Fig. 2a. The metal patch of the third layer includes a pair of arcs and a rectangular strip, while the metal patches of the first and fifth layers feature a pair of symmetric arcs. Additionally, these layers are equipped with stepping motors to effectively control the three-layer insulator structure (see Fig. 2c). To avoid friction and collision during rotation, we designed the insulator to be circular, with a diameter slightly smaller than the edge length of the square metal backplate. This design dimension is adequate to meet the requirements for the stepper motors to drive the rotation of each insulating layer. Due to the total reflection characteristics of the metallic backplane, the impact of the motor on the unit characteristics can be neglected.

The rotational angles of two layers with respect to the rectangular strip are γ1 and κ1, respectively (see more details in the “Methods” section). When γ1 is set equal to κ1, the structure becomes centrosymmetric, permitting it to rotate around its central axis of symmetry. The designed meta-atom achieves highly efficient polarization conversion by exploiting strong anisotropy and limits the internal resonance field to minimize the coupling between adjacent units. Theoretically, a rotation of the meta-atom around its central axis, perpendicular to the z-axis by an angle α (as depicted in Fig. 2b), would result in a phase change of the reflection coefficients RRR and RLL. Based on the Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase theory, this phase change is equal to 2α. Here, RRR and RLL represent the reflection coefficients for RCP and LCP incident waves converted to their corresponding co-polarization reflected waves, respectively, and α denotes the overall rotation angle of the meta-atom.

To assess the reflective capabilities of the proposed reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom under a linearly polarized incident wave, numerical simulations are performed. Supplementary Fig. 19b, c illustrates the simulated amplitude and phase responses of the reflection coefficients RUU, RUV, RVU, RVV of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom (see Supplementary Fig. 22a) with γ=κ=90°, γ1=κ1=0°, and α=0° in the frequency range from 1 to 8 GHz. Here, reference coordinates {U, V} denote the principal axes of the local coordinate systems of the meta-atom, and Rij signifies the complex reflection amplitude for the incoming EM waves with linear polarization along the j-axis and the outgoing waves with linear polarization along the i-axis, where i, j ∈ {U, V}. The elements of the Jones matrix R(0) are not entirely independent but are constrained by the symmetry of the meta-atom54. According to group theory, if a structure is invariant under a particular symmetric operation characterized by operator G, then the matrix R(0) will also be invariant under this operation, mathematically expressed as GR(0)G−1=R(0). Considering that the meta-atom has mirror symmetry with respect to its principal axis, we have the matrix G = [1 0; 0 -1], which necessitates that RUV=RVU=0, as verified by Supplementary Fig. 22b, c. In addition, the system studied in our work exhibits time-reversal symmetry, and the proposed reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is mirror-symmetric. Based on the law of energy conservation, it can be inferred that the coefficients RUU and RVV are approximately equal in magnitude.

The meta-atom displayed in Supplementary Fig. 22a undergoes 135° counter-clockwise rotation around the z-axis, resulting in the transformation of the incident plane wave from linear to circular polarization, as shown in Fig. 2d. Following this, we further study the reflection responses of the proposed meta-atom. Figure 2e and Supplementary Fig. 19d showcase the theoretically predicted results and numerically simulated results of the reflection coefficients RRR, RLR, RRL, RLL. We remark that the theoretically predicted results are based on analytical values derived from the Jones matrix transformations, as detailed in Supplementary Note 13, whereas the numerically simulated results are obtained by using the full-wave simulations. The simulated amplitudes and phases are depicted with crimson and azure lines, respectively, and the theoretical estimations for amplitudes and phases are indicated by red squares and blue diamond dots. We observe that there is agreement between the theoretical calculations and numerical simulations.

The Poincaré sphere enables a straightforward depiction of all possible polarization states. Each point on the sphere represents a specific polarization state, where the north and south poles indicate the right-circular polarization (|RCP〉) state and left-circular polarization (|LCP〉) state, respectively. The points along the equator illustrate the linear polarization (|LP〉) states, and those elsewhere indicate elliptical polarization (|EP〉) states. The Poincaré sphere provides an insightful visualization of the evolution process of the polarization from one state to another. As shown in Fig. 2f, under the illumination of an RCP plane wave, the reflected field is numerically calculated to trace the transformation trajectory of polarization on the Poincaré sphere. In the incident region, the polarization state of the EM wave remains RCP along the whole incident propagation path. This state is referred to as the initial state, which is marked with a red circle on the Poincaré sphere in Fig. 2g.

In the reflected region, the incident EM wave interacts with the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom, leading to significant changes in polarization state. This reflected polarization state gradually evolves along the reflected propagation path and eventually settles into a stable state. We define this stable polarization state as the final state, depicted with a purple dot on the Poincaré sphere. The transition of the polarization state of the reflected wave is visualized with a sequence of smaller red dots, each of which represents a specific transition state. The theoretical values of the final state of the reflected wave are further derived using Eq. (S3) or (S5). These values are represented with a green circle on the Poincaré sphere. The strong alignment between the purple and green circles further confirms the validity of our geometric representation of the proposed theory of analog superposition states in reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces. While our research primarily focuses on the final polarization state in the far field, the polarization transformation in the near field is also very helpful for gaining a deeper understanding of the physics behind how the proposed metasurface works55,56. Additionally, we examine the polarization evolution under LCP plane wave incidence, as demonstrated in Fig. 2h, i, and determine the expected final state using Eq. (S4) to enhance the reliability.

In order to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the analog superposition state in mathematical and geometric representations, we conducted a wideband validation at multiple frequency points. This approach aims to overcome the inherent limitation in the geometric representation of the analog superposition state on the Poincaré sphere, which is defined to analogously mimic the superposition state properties of a quantum bit at a single frequency point. Here, we should note that the Poincaré sphere is capable of representing polarization states across multiple frequencies, with each point on the sphere corresponding to a polarization state at one frequency. This enables the characterization of a spectrum of polarization states. From an application perspective, the analog superposition states in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface are expected to be effective over a wide frequency spectrum, rather than being limited to one specific frequency point. Analog superposition state of reconfigurable metasurfaces in classical systems
As the fundamental units of information in quantum information theory, the quantum bits exhibit two primary features: superposition57 and entanglement58,59. Drawing inspiration from the distinct representation of the quantum-bit superposition states on the Bloch sphere, here we study the analog superposition state in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface on the Poincaré sphere (with built details provided in the Supplementary Note 1). Equations (S3) and (S4) demonstrate that the polarization state of the EM waves reflected by a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is determined by two degrees of freedom on the Poincaré sphere, namely θ and ϕ, as illustrated in Fig. 1d. Under the excitation of circularly polarized plane waves, we find that the resonant frequency of the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface shifts towards lower frequencies as the equivalent arc length of the meta-atom increases. Here, the equivalent arc length refers to the longer arc distance between the ends of the first and fifth curved metallic layers with respect to the central longitudinal axis of the third rectangular strip, with their numerical values given by (γ1+γ2)/2 and (κ1+κ2)/2, respectively.

As a result, by maintaining a constant overall rotation angle α and adjusting the relative rotation angles γ1 and κ1, it is feasible to achieve a complete transition of |RRR| from 1 to 0, while keeping fRRR unchanged at a specific frequency. This feature enables a flexible scanning of the polarization states along the latitude of the Poincaré sphere with the latitude angle θ from 0 to π while keeping the longitude angle ϕ constant, as shown in Fig. 3a, e. The agreement between full-wave simulations and theoretical predictions is validated in Fig. 3c, g (see more details of the result comparison in Supplementary Table 1). This also makes it possible to flexibly manipulate the analog superposition state of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom along the latitude of the Poincaré sphere by maintaining its rotation angle α=0° and tuning the relative rotation angles (γ1 and κ1) within a certain range, as depicted in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 23.

Since the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is designed from the PB phase, one can control the polarization evolution path of the reflected wave by manipulating the overall rotation angle α of the meta-atom. Our results show that the PB phase is only dependent on the rotation angle of the meta-atom and can achieve a phase coverage from 0 to 2π. We also find that the reflected wave generated by the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface can induce a longitude-angle change (Δϕ) on the Poincaré sphere, namely Δϕ=±2Δα. Hence, when the equivalent arc length of the meta-atom structure remains the same, the longitude angle ϕ can traverse from 0° to 360° by adjusting the rotation angle α from 0° to 180°, whilst maintaining the latitude angle θ constant.

To support our findings, we have conducted both numerical simulations and theoretical predictions, as shown in Fig. 3d, h. The excellent agreement between the numerical simulations and theoretical predictions of the final polarization states of reflected waves generated by a metasurface composed of periodically arranged meta-atoms under circularly polarized excitation confirms the accuracy of the proposed theory (see more numerical data in Supplementary Table 2). It merits emphasis that our theory is based on linear polarization, whereas the simulations directly pertain to circular polarization, indicating a distinction between the roots of the two. Moreover, the theory offers a swift and exceedingly precise analytical method unmatched by simulations for determining the final polarization state on the Poincaré sphere. This method not only avoids the complications associated with electric field simulations and subsequent processing (as depicted in Supplementary Fig. 1) but also simplifies experimental assessments and analytical processes. Furthermore, by adjusting the overall rotation angle α and fixing the relative rotation angles (γ1 and κ1) of each reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom, we can map the final polarization state of the reflected wave along the latitude lines on the Poincaré sphere, as illustrated in Fig. 3b, f and Supplementary Fig. 24a, b. Due to the inherent tunability of the proposed meta-atom, the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom can have infinite rotation configurations. Under a given rotation configuration, the EM response (i.e., the final polarization state of the reflected wave) of the meta-atom will always be mapped to a specific point on the Poincaré sphere. To realize the analog superposition state in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface, it is crucial to traverse all possible polarization states on the Poincaré sphere. By manipulating the rotation configuration of the proposed meta-atom, we can flexibly scan the final polarization states of the reflected wave across the Poincaré sphere’s longitude and latitude. This allows us to construct the analog superposition states on the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. It should be noted that the analog superposition states have been explored and validated under the condition of normal incidence with circularly polarized waves. A detailed discussion on the impact of different polarizations and incidence angles on the performance of the analog superposition states is presented in the Supplementary Note 7.

Analog nonseparable state of reconfigurable metasurfaces in classical systems
Entanglement is a distinctive phenomenon in quantum mechanics, including the inter-system entanglement and intra-system entanglement. Both types of entanglement are characterized by the non-separable connection between states. In the classical systems, it is not feasible to achieve the inter-system entanglement. In contrast, the intra-system entanglement can be explored in the classical systems by investigating the inseparability among various degrees of freedom in a single system, and it is well-known as the classical entanglement.

To characterize the analog nonseparable states of space-polarization60,61 in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces, we study different degrees of freedom (such as the polarization and spatial modes) in EM systems to demonstrate the analog nonseparable correlation. Due to the spin-conjugate symmetry of the left- and right-handed PB phases, we can establish an analog nonseparable state based on the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom. We further introduce the concept of coding metasurface, wherein the coding inseparability always maintain a mutual correlation between the coding patterns of both spin states, as illustrated in Fig. 4a, c. A detailed examination of the structures, phases, and amplitude responses for four meta-atoms applied in 2-bit encoding is presented in Supplementary Fig. 2. Essentially, the meta-atoms remain unchanged in parameters, leading to uniform amplitude responses. In terms of phase differences, the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms assign the phase coding states of 0, 1, 2, and 3 to the spin-up ∇+90°|R〉 and spin-down ∇−90°|R〉. Inversely, the coding states of 3, 2, 1, and 0 are naturally assigned to the spin-down ∇−90°|L〉 and spin-up ∇+90°|L〉, respectively, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2c, d.

Illuminated by the incident EM wave with horizontally linear polarization, the scattering field patterns of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms exhibit an analog nonseparable state between the spin (polarization) and far-field spatial modes, as shown in Fig. 4b, d. For coding pattern 1, the beams corresponding to the spin-up and spin-down states occur at the spatial modes (11.0°, 0°) and (−11.0°, 180°), which are exactly aligned with the theoretical prediction results of (11.0°, 0°) and (−11.0°, 180°). Coding pattern 2 demonstrate similar results. In addition, the calculated Schmidt numbers (K) for both cases are 2, indicating that the polarization (spin) and spatial modes reach the maximum entanglement degree. Hence, we validate that an analog nonseparable state between the spin and far-field spatial modes can be implemented in the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms. Moreover, the resultant spin splitting phenomenon can be interpreted as a classical EM wave analog of the spin Hall effect.

Experimental demonstration of reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces
To experimentally demonstrate that the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is capable of characterizing the analog superposition state to yield an analog of the qubit superposition state, we fabricate a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface by setting γ=κ=90°. More details of these devices and their associated testing procedures are provided in the “Methods” section. Figure 5b, c presents the polarization conversion efficiencies and the positions (θ, ϕ) of the final polarization states of the reflected waves on the Poincaré sphere for different samples (see Fig. 5a) in a broad frequency band, respectively. Meanwhile, the corresponding geometric representations at a specific frequency of 5.33 GHz are depicted in Fig. 5d.

As verified in Fig. 5c, there is a notable concordance between the numerically simulated and experimentally measured results, regardless of the same rotation angle with different equivalent arc lengths (samples 1 and 2), or different rotation angles with the same equivalent arc lengths (samples 1 and 3). Such an agreement provides more reliable evidence to validate the accuracy of the mathematical and geometric representations for the analog superposition state in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. It should be noted that while our reconfigurable time-varying metasurface demonstrates effectiveness based on a mechanical modulation approach, the modulation speed is inherently dependent on the performance of the motors used (i.e., on the millisecond scale). In practical applications, as the complexity of the applications increases, we may not be limited to the analog superposition states or analog nonseparable states at a single frequency, leading to a heightened demand for increased modulation speeds. In fact, the existing literature has reported various faster modulation methods, such as electrical or optical tuning approaches. However, realizing the concept of the quantum-inspired bits requires to meet four necessary conditions, which cannot be achieved by the current reports. Therefore, in this initial attempt, we just realized the functionality. For a more detailed comparison between this work and the related studies, please refer to Supplementary Note 17. This section only includes experimental results for three cases. ## Methods

Meta-atom design and metasurface fabrication
Our proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is structured with separately and periodically arranged meta-atoms. The characteristics of these meta-atoms are optimized through rigorous numerical simulations and experimental evaluations. The geometric parameters of these meta-atoms are detailed in Fig. 2.

The metallic structure was fabricated by using printed circuit board (PCB) techniques. The F4B dielectric substrate used in this construction is circular and has three insulating layers. The thicknesses of the layers are h=3mm, h1=h2=0.254mm. The substrate has a radius of R1=9.7mm and a relative permittivity of 2.65. With a notably low loss tangent of 0.001, the substrate ensures optimal performance. The substrate is mounted atop a square and metallic plane with periodic side lengths of p=20mm. The construct is designed with multi-layered metallic motifs on the surface and a foundational backplate made of copper. The thickness of each layer is 18μm. The third layer hosts an array of metallic patches, each with an outer radius of R=4.6mm and an inner radius of 3.3mm. The geometrical parameters of the metal patches in the first- and fifth-layers mirror those of the arc segments in the third layer, while the rectangular strip width matches the arc width. Meta-atoms are arranged with center-to-center spacings of 20mm along both the x and y axes, maintaining a minimum gap of 0.6mm between them. Such a configuration allows for the free rotational movement of each meta-atom. Furthermore, each meta-atom is equipped with a motor for rotation control. The optimized dimensions of the meta-atoms fully accommodate the spatial requirements for independent rotational control of the insulating layers corresponding to each stepper motor. In the experimental setup, the prototype metasurface was constructed, comprising a matrix of 576 individually rotatable meta-atoms. The expansive metallic backplane covers an area of 570×560mm2. We also provide a detailed fabrication approach and corresponding experimental strategy in the Supplementary Note 16 for further research and applications.

Simulations
Rigorous numerical simulations throughout this study were performed using commercial software, CST Microwave Studio. In the mechanical modulation approach employed here, the control speed is much lower than the EM wave propagation speed. Thus, this scenario can be treated as a quasi-static EM problem. Consequently, in the numerical simulations, both analog superposition states and analog nonseparable states of the quantum-inspired bits synthesized in the time dimension were treated as static, eliminating the need for time-varying modeling. The analog superposition properties of the meta-atoms were numerically simulated using their frequency-domain solver. The simulations were conducted by imposing unit cell boundary conditions along the x and y axes, while using open-space boundary conditions along the z-axis. Meanwhile, the time-domain solver was employed to investigate the analog nonseparable state in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface, which was simulated by applying open boundary conditions in all three axes (x, y, and z). It should be noted that the analog nonseparable state simulation featured in Fig. 4 is operated at a frequency of 9.80 GHz. The dual coding patterns illustrated in Fig. 4a, c, were periodically structured in the x-axis, while preserving a fixed orientation along the y-axis. Each coding element is structured as a supercell composed of two identical units, resulting in a periodicity denoted as Γ, spanning a distance of 160mm.

Experiments
The experimental system is demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 3a, where the fabricated metasurface is housed in a compact microwave anechoic chamber. The measurement system includes two identical linearly polarized broadband horn antennas (GJ-WRDHA-U8/08-N) and a vector network analyzer (VNA) (Agilent N5230C). The two antennas are connected to the two ports of the VNA, serving as the feeding and receiving terminals, respectively. These two antennas are aligned at oblique angles of ±5° to measure the normal reflected EM waves, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3b. Antennas are placed 1m distant from the metasurface. The reflection coefficients ruu, ruv, rvu, rvv of the two metasurface prototypes were carefully measured at different rotational angles by using the time-domain gate innovations provided by the VNA. Transformation calculations predicated on Eqs. (S3) and (S4) were executed to obtain test results for θ and ϕ at each rotational angle. These methodologies contribute to an in-depth understanding of the reflective characteristics of the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces.

[Introduction]
In recent years, the continuous advancement of quantum mechanics1-3 has drawn increasing
attention to the field of quantum information science. As a revolutionary discipline bridging
quantum physics and information science, quantum information science4-6 is poised to
transform scientific and technological paradigms due to its immense application potential and
advantages. Specifically, quantum communication7-10 ensures the security of information
based on the principles of quantum physics, while quantum computing11-14 offers
computational capabilities that surpass those of classical computers, driving revolutions in
materials science, chemistry, and biomedicine. Furthermore, advancements in quantum
sensing15-18 and measurement19-21 technologies have significantly enhanced the performance
of traditional sensing and measurement systems.
The allure of quantum information science has not only catalyzed the development of
quantum metasurfaces22-25 but also fostered the flourishing of quantum optics26,27.
Metasurfaces28-32 are planar artificial structures composed of subwavelength unit cells,
designed in a periodic or non-periodic arrangement. Although initial metasurfaces lacked the
ability to modify electromagnetic (EM) responses post-fabrication33,34, which limited their
practical applications, researchers have proposed the concept of reconfigurable metasurfaces
as a solution to this limitation35-38. In contrast to traditional classical metasurfaces,
quantum metasurfaces represent a significant advancement, providing a critical research platform for
generating, manipulating, and detecting non-classical EM waves. However, the stringent
conditions required for the fabrication, manipulation, and testing of quantum metasurfaces
currently pose significant challenges to their practicality.
Concurrently, the concept of digital coding metasurfaces39 has evolved into that of
information metasurfaces40-48, bridging the realms of classical physics and information
science. While the basic information processing units of information metasurfaces are based
on classical bits, which offer stability, ease of storage and transmission, and straightforward
operation, they exhibit limitations in scalability and parallel processing capabilities. In
contrast, quantum bits49-51 present unprecedented advantages in computational speed and
parallelism, enabling the resolution of complex problems that classical bits cannot tackle.
Nevertheless, quantum bits are often unstable, making storage and transmission challenging,
and they are highly sensitive to environmental disturbances, necessitating complex error
correction techniques. Consequently, implementing their advantages within classical systems
remains a formidable challenge. This underscores the need for a feasible physical platform
capable of mimicking the characteristics of quantum bits while achieving a high degree of
computational freedom in stable classical EM systems. The concept of quantum-inspired
metamaterials52,53 provides a promising avenue for addressing this challenge.

## Paper

## Abstract

Classical and quantum bits serve as cornerstone in information science. As this field rapidly evolves, the interplay between the two continues to enrich and inspire each other. Here, analog superposition states and analog nonseparable states are theoretically explored and experimentally demonstrated in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. To implement the quantum-inspired states in classical system, we have developed a reconfigurable metasurface capable of synthesizing analog superposition states across the temporal dimension and analog nonseparable states across spatial and polarization dimensions. Due to its unique features of analog superposition and non-separability, the proposed metasurface holds great potential to revolutionize the information processing capabilities beyond those offered by the classical information metasurface. This work not only offers a reconfigurable physical platform to advance classical and quantum information, but also will both enable unknown wave phenomena and provide promising perspectives in the fields of information science, quantum physics and material science.

---

## Introduction

In recent years, the rapid advancement of quantum mechanics1–3 has attracted increasing attention to the field of quantum information science4–6. As an interdisciplinary discipline bridging quantum physics and information science, quantum information science is transforming research paradigms in both science and technology with its substantial practical potential and unique capabilities. Specifically, quantum communication7–10 leverages the phenomenon of quantum entanglement to ensure the security of information communication, whereas quantum computation11–14 exploits the principle of quantum superposition to achieve computational power that surpasses that of classical computers, thereby driving transformative advances in fields of materials science, chemistry, and beyond. Furthermore, the recent progress in quantum sensing15–18 and measurement19–21 technologies has significantly improved the performance of traditional sensors and measurement systems to unprecedented levels.

The success of quantum information science has not only stimulated the flourishing of quantum optics22,23, but has also propelled the development of quantum metasurfaces24–27. Metasurfaces are planar artificial structures composed of subwavelength meta-atoms arranged in either periodic or aperiodic configurations28–32. However, most passive metasurfaces lack the capability to reconfigure their electromagnetic (EM) functionality once fabricated33,34, which significantly limits their practical applications. To address this challenge, the concept of reconfigurable metasurfaces35–38 has been introduced. The switching capabilities of the EM response in reconfigurable metasurfaces have motivated the development of the digital metasurfaces39 and subsequently evolved into information metasurfaces40–48, which serve to bridge information science and classical EM physics.

The basic information-processing units of information metasurfaces are based on classical digital bits, which offer benefits such as stability, ease of storage and transmission, and operational simplicity. However, they suffer from limitations in information capacity and parallel-processing capability. In contrast, quantum bits (qubits)49–51 exhibit unprecedented superiority in these aspects, offering potential solutions to address the challenges currently faced by classical digital bits. However, qubits are often unstable, difficult to store and transmit, and highly susceptible to environmental interference. To combine the respective advantages of classical bits and qubits, several attempts are being made to develop quantum-inspired bits52,53 in classical systems. Nevertheless, current studies are mostly limited to theoretical explorations, and the experimental realization and manipulation of quantum-inspired states in classical systems remain a significant challenge in this field.

In this work, we investigate the quantum-inspired states of reconfigurable metasurfaces to emulate the mathematical and geometrical representations of the quantum states. We should clarify that the quantum-inspired states discussed here are implemented in a classical system rather than in a quantum system. Generally, the mathematical representation provides a theoretical framework to rigorously describe the quantum-inspired states, whereas the geometric representation offers an intuitive way to understand them. Specifically, we initiate our discussions by introducing the concept and mathematical framework of the analog superposition state to explore the analog superposition behavior of the EM waves based on a reconfigurable metasurface in a classical system. To validate the correctness of our theoretical model, we perform numerical simulations on the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. All numerical simulations were conducted based on the fundamental frequency, without considering the influence of other harmonic frequencies. Each meta-atom on the metasurface can be individually controlled through mechanical rotation, thereby enabling flexible manipulation of the polarization state on the Poincaré sphere. Notably, the reconfigurable feature of the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface allows it to transform the polarization state by reaching all possible points on the Poincaré sphere, which is a crucial ability to implement the analog superposition state. We further demonstrate an analog nonseparable state that mirrors the entanglement between light spin and far-field spatial modes. In a proof-of-concept experiment, we show excellent agreement between the experimental results and numerical simulations, thus affirming that the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is a feasible platform to realize the concept of quantum-inspired states. We believe that the introduction of the quantum-inspired bit and the realization of the reconfigurable array platform will advance the developments in various fields, including quantum physics, information science, and metamaterials.

---

## Results

Reconfigurable time-varying metasurface
We commence our analysis by investigating the EM properties of various meta-atoms to explore the correlations among different information bit types. In classical information processing, a classical bit is generally represented by the binary state 0 or 1. Physically, these classical bits are inherently binary systems, distinguished by their exclusive occupation of one of two possible states. The EM properties of the meta-atom in the classical information metasurfaces are controlled by a binary state, namely the coding state 0 (ON) or 1 (OFF), by switching the PIN diode, as depicted in Fig. 1a. Mathematically, the binary state can be formulated as |Ψ〉=(1−δ)|0〉+δ|1〉, where |0〉 and |1〉 denote the respective reflection polarization states (i.e., |Ψ〉) of the meta-atom when the PIN diode is in its ON (δ=0) and OFF (δ=1) configurations, with δ being restricted to 0 or 1. It is noteworthy that the operations involving the classical bits are deterministic, complying with Boolean algebra principles. In the classical context, the classical bits are limited to process a single state at any given moment. In contrast, the quantum bits leverage the superposition property to provide significant advantages in parallel information processing. Generally, the Bloch sphere is used as a geometric representation to succinctly and clearly convey this concept, as depicted in Fig. 1b. In this representation, the state of a quantum bit can be visualized at any location on the Bloch sphere, transcending the limitations of classical information processing.

The mathematical representation of a quantum bit can be expressed as a linear superposition of two polarization states, namely |Ψ〉=α|0〉+β|1〉. The coefficients, α and β, are complex numbers that are subjected to normalization and probabilistic constraints |α|2+|β|2=1. After initializing the global phase to zero and defining the relative phase as ϕ, the state |Ψ〉 has only two degrees of freedom. The Bloch sphere surface, which represents the qubit state space, is inherently two-dimensional, providing two distinct local degrees of freedom. As a result, this state can be mathematically represented by |Ψi= cosθ|0i+eiϕ sinθ|1i. In this context, the polar angle θ (ranging from 0 to π) and the azimuthal angle ϕ (from 0 to 2π) correspondingly denote the quantum bit’s position on the Bloch sphere, akin to the latitude and longitude. With the determination of θ and ϕ, the quantum state is fully defined and can be geometrically represented.

Inspired by the mathematical and geometric representations of quantum bits, here we introduce a concept of quantum-inspired bits (as shown in Fig. 1b), the state of which can be mathematically expressed as an analog superposition state:
|Ψi= cosθ|Ri+eiϕ sinθ|Li. Here, |R〉 and |L〉 represent two orthogonal bases that constitute the bit: right-handed circular polarization (RCP) and left-handed circular polarization (LCP) states. This mathematical representation is applicable to the RCP plane-wave incidence scenarios. For the LCP incidence, the coefficients associated with two orthogonal bases should be interchanged.

To implement the aforementioned analog superposition state, we propose a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface as a feasible physical platform. Additionally, the metasurface exhibits analog nonseparable state properties, as shown in Fig. 1c. Different from the conventional digital coding metasurface, the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface employs a discrete periodic configuration of meta-atoms, which are designed to overcome the rotation-related challenges, including friction and collisions between adjacent meta-atoms. We employ a multi-layered metal-insulator-metal spacer structure to design the meta-atom, optimizing their performance, and integrate stepping motors for actuation (details can be found in the “Methods” section), as illustrated in Fig. 1d. This structure facilitates the flexible control of the reflected wave’s polarization state over the Poincaré sphere through both forward and backward stepping and rotational stepping dimensions in practice. Given that the analog superposition state corresponds to the polarization state of the reflected wave, we opt to represent this using the Poincaré sphere rather than the Bloch sphere, as shown in Fig. 1b for more accurate visualization. We note that the realization of this concept essentially relies on the introduction of a temporal dimension and rotational transformations in the same reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom. In quantum physics, a qubit has an instant superposition of states. In our case, the analog superposition of states is implemented in a certain time interval on the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom by manipulating its rotation angle at different times. It is important to emphasize that both the time interval and the system’s response time remain on the order of milliseconds. In principle, minimizing the time interval towards zero would yield an analog of the qubit superposition state. More details of the theoretical derivations for the mathematical and geometric representations of the analog superposition state in reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces can be found in the Supplementary Note 1.

Reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom
The configuration of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is illustrated in Fig. 2a. The metal patch of the third layer includes a pair of arcs and a rectangular strip, while the metal patches of the first and fifth layers feature a pair of symmetric arcs. Additionally, these layers are equipped with stepping motors to effectively control the three-layer insulator structure (see Fig. 2c). To avoid friction and collision during rotation, we designed the insulator to be circular, with a diameter slightly smaller than the edge length of the square metal backplate. This design dimension is adequate to meet the requirements for the stepper motors to drive the rotation of each insulating layer. Due to the total reflection characteristics of the metallic backplane, the impact of the motor on the unit characteristics can be neglected.

The rotational angles of two layers with respect to the rectangular strip are γ1 and κ1, respectively (see more details in the “Methods” section). When γ1 is set equal to κ1, the structure becomes centrosymmetric, permitting it to rotate around its central axis of symmetry. The designed meta-atom achieves highly efficient polarization conversion by exploiting strong anisotropy and limits the internal resonance field to minimize the coupling between adjacent units. Theoretically, a rotation of the meta-atom around its central axis, perpendicular to the z-axis by an angle α (as depicted in Fig. 2b), would result in a phase change of the reflection coefficients RRR and RLL. Based on the Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase theory, this phase change is equal to 2α. Here, RRR and RLL represent the reflection coefficients for RCP and LCP incident waves converted to their corresponding co-polarization reflected waves, respectively, and α denotes the overall rotation angle of the meta-atom.

To assess the reflective capabilities of the proposed reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom under a linearly polarized incident wave, numerical simulations are performed. Supplementary Fig. 19b, c illustrates the simulated amplitude and phase responses of the reflection coefficients RUU, RUV, RVU, RVV of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom (see Supplementary Fig. 22a) with γ=κ=90°, γ1=κ1=0°, and α=0° in the frequency range from 1 to 8 GHz. Here, reference coordinates {U, V} denote the principal axes of the local coordinate systems of the meta-atom, and Rij signifies the complex reflection amplitude for the incoming EM waves with linear polarization along the j-axis and the outgoing waves with linear polarization along the i-axis, where i, j ∈ {U, V}. The elements of the Jones matrix R(0) are not entirely independent but are constrained by the symmetry of the meta-atom54. According to group theory, if a structure is invariant under a particular symmetric operation characterized by operator G, then the matrix R(0) will also be invariant under this operation, mathematically expressed as GR(0)G−1=R(0). Considering that the meta-atom has mirror symmetry with respect to its principal axis, we have the matrix G = [1 0; 0 -1], which necessitates that RUV=RVU=0, as verified by Supplementary Fig. 22b, c. In addition, the system studied in our work exhibits time-reversal symmetry, and the proposed reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is mirror-symmetric. Based on the law of energy conservation, it can be inferred that the coefficients RUU and RVV are approximately equal in magnitude.

The meta-atom displayed in Supplementary Fig. 22a undergoes 135° counter-clockwise rotation around the z-axis, resulting in the transformation of the incident plane wave from linear to circular polarization, as shown in Fig. 2d. Following this, we further study the reflection responses of the proposed meta-atom. Figure 2e and Supplementary Fig. 19d showcase the theoretically predicted results and numerically simulated results of the reflection coefficients RRR, RLR, RRL, RLL. We remark that the theoretically predicted results are based on analytical values derived from the Jones matrix transformations, as detailed in Supplementary Note 13, whereas the numerically simulated results are obtained by using the full-wave simulations. The simulated amplitudes and phases are depicted with crimson and azure lines, respectively, and the theoretical estimations for amplitudes and phases are indicated by red squares and blue diamond dots. We observe that there is agreement between the theoretical calculations and numerical simulations.

The Poincaré sphere enables a straightforward depiction of all possible polarization states. Each point on the sphere represents a specific polarization state, where the north and south poles indicate the right-circular polarization (|RCP〉) state and left-circular polarization (|LCP〉) state, respectively. The points along the equator illustrate the linear polarization (|LP〉) states, and those elsewhere indicate elliptical polarization (|EP〉) states. The Poincaré sphere provides an insightful visualization of the evolution process of the polarization from one state to another. As shown in Fig. 2f, under the illumination of an RCP plane wave, the reflected field is numerically calculated to trace the transformation trajectory of polarization on the Poincaré sphere. In the incident region, the polarization state of the EM wave remains RCP along the whole incident propagation path. This state is referred to as the initial state, which is marked with a red circle on the Poincaré sphere in Fig. 2g.

In the reflected region, the incident EM wave interacts with the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom, leading to significant changes in polarization state. This reflected polarization state gradually evolves along the reflected propagation path and eventually settles into a stable state. We define this stable polarization state as the final state, depicted with a purple dot on the Poincaré sphere. The transition of the polarization state of the reflected wave is visualized with a sequence of smaller red dots, each of which represents a specific transition state. In Fig. 2f, we present the polarization state of the reflected wave at eight equidistant positions to better illustrate the polarization evolution. The theoretical values of the final state of the reflected wave are further derived using Eq. (S3) or (S5). These values are represented with a green circle on the Poincaré sphere. The strong alignment between the purple and green circles further confirms the validity of our geometric representation of the proposed theory of analog superposition states in reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces. While our research primarily focuses on the final polarization state in the far field, the polarization transformation in the near field is also very helpful for gaining a deeper understanding of the physics behind how the proposed metasurface works55,56. Additionally, we examine the polarization evolution under LCP plane wave incidence, as demonstrated in Fig. 2h, i, and determine the expected final state using Eq. (S4) to enhance the reliability.

In order to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the analog superposition state in mathematical and geometric representations, we conducted a wideband validation at multiple frequency points. This approach aims to overcome the inherent limitation in the geometric representation of the analog superposition state on the Poincaré sphere, which is defined to analogously mimic the superposition state properties of a quantum bit at a single frequency point. Here, we should note that the Poincaré sphere is capable of representing polarization states across multiple frequencies, with each point on the sphere corresponding to a polarization state at one frequency. This enables the characterization of a spectrum of polarization states. From an application perspective, the analog superposition states in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface are expected to be effective over a wide frequency spectrum, rather than being limited to one specific frequency point. Further details on the broadband validation of the analog superposition state are available in the Supplementary Note 12. Supplementary Fig. 16a, d shows the conceptual diagrams of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms under the RCP and LCP plane-wave incidences, showcasing the polarization evolution path on the Poincaré sphere at an observation frequency of 5.35 GHz. It should be noted that the meta-atom and observation frequency in this scenario are consistent with those in Fig. 2f–i. We initially examined the circularly polarized reflection responses of the meta-atom by obtaining the theoretically predicted and numerically simulated results for the amplitude-frequency and phase-frequency responses, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 16b, c, e, f. Subsequently, we compare four reflection coefficients in the range from 1 to 8 GHz for the purpose of wideband validation, which are demonstrated in the histograms in Supplementary Fig. 16g–j.

Based on the mathematical values of the reflection coefficients, we display the geometric representation of the reflected polarization’s final state under RCP and LCP illuminations, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 17a, c (see the Supplementary Note 13 for the calculation formula). Meanwhile, we visually demonstrate the reflected polarization evolution paths on the Poincaré sphere in Supplementary Fig. 17b, d, where the theoretically predicted results and numerically simulated results of the reflection polarization’s final states are compared with the purple and green dots. The comparison of the results confirms the applicability and accuracy of both mathematical and geometric representations of analog superposition states in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface, supporting the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Analog superposition state of reconfigurable metasurfaces in classical systems
As the fundamental units of information in quantum information theory, the quantum bits exhibit two primary features: superposition57 and entanglement58,59. Drawing inspiration from the distinct representation of the quantum-bit superposition states on the Bloch sphere, here we study the analog superposition state in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface on the Poincaré sphere (with built details provided in the Supplementary Note 1). Equations (S3) and (S4) demonstrate that the polarization state of the EM waves reflected by a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is determined by two degrees of freedom on the Poincaré sphere, namely θ and ϕ, as illustrated in Fig. 1d. Under the excitation of circularly polarized plane waves, we find that the resonant frequency of the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface shifts towards lower frequencies as the equivalent arc length of the meta-atom increases. Here, the equivalent arc length refers to the longer arc distance between the ends of the first and fifth curved metallic layers with respect to the central longitudinal axis of the third rectangular strip, with their numerical values given by (γ1+γ2)/2 and (κ1+κ2)/2, respectively.

As a result, by maintaining a constant overall rotation angle α and adjusting the relative rotation angles γ1 and κ1, it is feasible to achieve a complete transition of |RRR| from 1 to 0, while keeping fRRR unchanged at a specific frequency. This feature enables a flexible scanning of the polarization states along the latitude of the Poincaré sphere with the latitude angle θ from 0 to π while keeping the longitude angle ϕ constant, as shown in Fig. 3a, e. The agreement between full-wave simulations and theoretical predictions is validated in Fig. 3c, g (see more details of the result comparison in Supplementary Table 1). This also makes it possible to flexibly manipulate the analog superposition state of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom along the latitude of the Poincaré sphere by maintaining its rotation angle α=0° and tuning the relative rotation angles (γ1 and κ1) within a certain range, as depicted in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 23.

Since the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom is designed from the PB phase, one can control the polarization evolution path of the reflected wave by manipulating the overall rotation angle α of the meta-atom. Our results show that the PB phase is only dependent on the rotation angle of the meta-atom and can achieve a phase coverage from 0 to 2π. We also find that the reflected wave generated by the reconfigurable time-varying metasurface can induce a longitude-angle change (Δϕ) on the Poincaré sphere, namely Δϕ=±2Δα. Hence, when the equivalent arc length of the meta-atom structure remains the same, the longitude angle ϕ can traverse from 0° to 360° by adjusting the rotation angle α from 0° to 180°, whilst maintaining the latitude angle θ constant.

To support our findings, we have conducted both numerical simulations and theoretical predictions, as shown in Fig. 3d, h. The excellent agreement between the numerical simulations and theoretical predictions of the final polarization states of reflected waves generated by a metasurface composed of periodically arranged meta-atoms under circularly polarized excitation confirms the accuracy of the proposed theory (see more numerical data in Supplementary Table 2). It merits emphasis that our theory is based on linear polarization, whereas the simulations directly pertain to circular polarization, indicating a distinction between the roots of the two. Moreover, the theory offers a swift and exceedingly precise analytical method unmatched by simulations for determining the final polarization state on the Poincaré sphere. This method not only avoids the complications associated with electric field simulations and subsequent processing (as depicted in Supplementary Fig. 1) but also simplifies experimental assessments and analytical processes. Furthermore, by adjusting the overall rotation angle α and fixing the relative rotation angles (γ1 and κ1) of each reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom, we can map the final polarization state of the reflected wave along the latitude lines on the Poincaré sphere, as illustrated in Fig. 3b, f and Supplementary Fig. 24a, b. Due to the inherent tunability of the proposed meta-atom, the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom can have infinite rotation configurations. Under a given rotation configuration, the EM response (i.e., the final polarization state of the reflected wave) of the meta-atom will always be mapped to a specific point on the Poincaré sphere. To realize the analog superposition state in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface, it is crucial to traverse all possible polarization states on the Poincaré sphere. By manipulating the rotation configuration of the proposed meta-atom, we can flexibly scan the final polarization states of the reflected wave across the Poincaré sphere’s longitude and latitude. This allows us to construct the analog superposition states on the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. It should be noted that the analog superposition states have been explored and validated under the condition of normal incidence with circularly polarized waves. A detailed discussion on the impact of different polarizations and incidence angles on the performance of the analog superposition states is presented in the Supplementary Note 7.

Analog nonseparable state of reconfigurable metasurfaces in classical systems
Entanglement is a distinctive phenomenon in quantum mechanics, including the inter-system entanglement and intra-system entanglement. Both types of entanglement are characterized by the non-separable connection between states. In the classical systems, it is not feasible to achieve the inter-system entanglement. In contrast, the intra-system entanglement can be explored in the classical systems by investigating the inseparability among various degrees of freedom in a single system, and it is well-known as the classical entanglement.

To characterize the analog nonseparable states of space-polarization60,61 in the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces, we study different degrees of freedom (such as the polarization and spatial modes) in EM systems to demonstrate the analog nonseparable correlation. Due to the spin-conjugate symmetry of the left- and right-handed PB phases, we can establish an analog nonseparable state based on the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atom. We further introduce the concept of coding metasurface, wherein the coding inseparability always maintain a mutual correlation between the coding patterns of both spin states, as illustrated in Fig. 4a, c. A detailed examination of the structures, phases, and amplitude responses for four meta-atoms applied in 2-bit encoding is presented in Supplementary Fig. 2. Essentially, the meta-atoms remain unchanged in parameters, leading to uniform amplitude responses. In terms of phase differences, the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms assign the phase coding states of 0, 1, 2, and 3 to the spin-up ∇+90°|R〉 and spin-down ∇−90°|R〉. Inversely, the coding states of 3, 2, 1, and 0 are naturally assigned to the spin-down ∇−90°|L〉 and spin-up ∇+90°|L〉, respectively, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2c, d.

Illuminated by the incident EM wave with horizontally linear polarization, the scattering field patterns of the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms exhibit an analog nonseparable state between the spin (polarization) and far-field spatial modes, as shown in Fig. 4b, d. For coding pattern 1, the beams corresponding to the spin-up and spin-down states occur at the spatial modes (11.0°, 0°) and (−11.0°, 180°), which are exactly aligned with the theoretical prediction results of (11.0°, 0°) and (−11.0°, 180°). Coding pattern 2 demonstrate similar results. In addition, the calculated Schmidt numbers (K) for both cases are 2, indicating that the polarization (spin) and spatial modes reach the maximum entanglement degree. Hence, we validate that an analog nonseparable state between the spin and far-field spatial modes can be implemented in the reconfigurable time-varying meta-atoms. Moreover, the resultant spin splitting phenomenon can be interpreted as a classical EM wave analog of the spin Hall effect.

Experimental demonstration of reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces
To experimentally demonstrate that the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is capable of characterizing the analog superposition state to yield an analog of the qubit superposition state, we fabricate a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface by setting γ=κ=90°. More details of these devices and their associated testing procedures are provided in the “Methods” section. Figure 5b, c presents the polarization conversion efficiencies and the positions (θ, ϕ) of the final polarization states of the reflected waves on the Poincaré sphere for different samples (see Fig. 5a) in a broad frequency band, respectively. Meanwhile, the corresponding geometric representations at a specific frequency of 5.33 GHz are depicted in Fig. 5d.

As verified in Fig. 5c, there is a notable concordance between the numerically simulated and experimentally measured results, regardless of the same rotation angle with different equivalent arc lengths (samples 1 and 2), or different rotation angles with the same equivalent arc lengths (samples 1 and 3). Such an agreement provides more reliable evidence to validate the accuracy of the mathematical and geometric representations for the analog superposition state in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface. It should be noted that while our reconfigurable time-varying metasurface demonstrates effectiveness based on a mechanical modulation approach, the modulation speed is inherently dependent on the performance of the motors used (i.e., on the millisecond scale). In practical applications, as the complexity of the applications increases, we may not be limited to the analog superposition states or analog nonseparable states at a single frequency, leading to a heightened demand for increased modulation speeds. In fact, the existing literature has reported various faster modulation methods, such as electrical or optical tuning approaches. However, realizing the concept of the quantum-inspired bits requires to meet four necessary conditions, which cannot be achieved by the current reports. Therefore, in this initial attempt, we just realized the functionality. For a more detailed comparison between this work and the related studies, please refer to Supplementary Note 17. This section only includes experimental results for three cases. Additional experimental results and more relevant discussions (including the polarization conversion efficiency, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and fidelity) are provided in the Supplementary Notes 8 and 9. Furthermore, we provide a more detailed experimental strategy to achieve more flexible control in the Supplementary Note 16.

## Methods

Meta-atom design and metasurface fabrication
Our proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurface is structured with separately and periodically arranged meta-atoms. The characteristics of these meta-atoms are optimized through rigorous numerical simulations and experimental evaluations. The geometric parameters of these meta-atoms are detailed in Fig. 2.

The metallic structure was fabricated by using printed circuit board (PCB) techniques. The F4B dielectric substrate used in this construction is circular and has three insulating layers. The thicknesses of the layers are h=3mm, h1=h2=0.254mm. The substrate has a radius of R1=9.7mm and a relative permittivity of 2.65. With a notably low loss tangent of 0.001, the substrate ensures optimal performance. The substrate is mounted atop a square and metallic plane with periodic side lengths of p=20mm. The construct is designed with multi-layered metallic motifs on the surface and a foundational backplate made of copper. The thickness of each layer is 18μm. The third layer hosts an array of metallic patches, each with an outer radius of R=4.6mm and an inner radius of 3.3mm. The geometrical parameters of the metal patches in the first- and fifth-layers mirror those of the arc segments in the third layer, while the rectangular strip width matches the arc width. Meta-atoms are arranged with center-to-center spacings of 20mm along both the x and y axes, maintaining a minimum gap of 0.6mm between them. Such a configuration allows for the free rotational movement of each meta-atom. Furthermore, each meta-atom is equipped with a motor for rotation control. The optimized dimensions of the meta-atoms fully accommodate the spatial requirements for independent rotational control of the insulating layers corresponding to each stepper motor. In the experimental setup, the prototype metasurface was constructed, comprising a matrix of 576 individually rotatable meta-atoms. The expansive metallic backplane covers an area of 570×560mm2. We also provide a detailed fabrication approach and corresponding experimental strategy in the Supplementary Note 16 for further research and applications.

Simulations
Rigorous numerical simulations throughout this study were performed using commercial software, CST Microwave Studio. In the mechanical modulation approach employed here, the control speed is much lower than the EM wave propagation speed. Thus, this scenario can be treated as a quasi-static EM problem. Consequently, in the numerical simulations, both analog superposition states and analog nonseparable states of the quantum-inspired bits synthesized in the time dimension were treated as static, eliminating the need for time-varying modeling. The analog superposition properties of the meta-atoms were numerically simulated using their frequency-domain solver. The simulations were conducted by imposing unit cell boundary conditions along the x and y axes, while using open-space boundary conditions along the z-axis. Meanwhile, the time-domain solver was employed to investigate the analog nonseparable state in a reconfigurable time-varying metasurface, which was simulated by applying open boundary conditions in all three axes (x, y, and z). It should be noted that the analog nonseparable state simulation featured in Fig. 4 is operated at a frequency of 9.80 GHz. The dual coding patterns illustrated in Fig. 4a, c, were periodically structured in the x-axis, while preserving a fixed orientation along the y-axis. Each coding element is structured as a supercell composed of two identical units, resulting in a periodicity denoted as Γ, spanning a distance of 160mm.

Experiments
The experimental system is demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 3a, where the fabricated metasurface is housed in a compact microwave anechoic chamber. The measurement system includes two identical linearly polarized broadband horn antennas (GJ-WRDHA-U8/08-N) and a vector network analyzer (VNA) (Agilent N5230C). The two antennas are connected to the two ports of the VNA, serving as the feeding and receiving terminals, respectively. These two antennas are aligned at oblique angles of ±5° to measure the normal reflected EM waves, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3b. Antennas are placed 1m distant from the metasurface. The reflection coefficients ruu, ruv, rvu, rvv of the two metasurface prototypes were carefully measured at different rotational angles by using the time-domain gate innovations provided by the VNA. Transformation calculations predicated on Eqs. (S3) and (S4) were executed to obtain test results for θ and ϕ at each rotational angle. These methodologies contribute to an in-depth understanding of the reflective characteristics of the proposed reconfigurable time-varying metasurfaces.

Our research primarily focuses on mimicking specific quantum effects within a classical
framework, particularly using quantum bits (qubits) as the core subject of study. To effectively
mimic the characteristics of qubits, we introduced a new concept termed “quantum-inspired
bit,” aimed at modeling superposition and entangled states. This concept represents a
significant innovation in our research, as our primary objective is not solely to achieve
polarization conversion. In the field of quantum information, qubits serve as the fundamental
units of information processing; however, their practical applications face numerous
challenges, including difficulties in preparation, stringent experimental conditions, complex
operations, and susceptibility to collapse. Thus, we aim to achieve a robust bit similar to
qubits within a classical framework, namely the quantum-inspired bit.
Furthermore, our research is inspired by the “information metasurface” concept first
proposed in 2014, initially aimed at facilitating digital encoding in metasurfaces and
subsequently extended to the field of information metasurfaces. Although the basic processing
unit of information metasurfaces remains classical bits, the limitations of classical bit capacity
have prompted us to explore the potential of quantum-inspired bits for achieving higher
information capacity. It is based on this dual consideration that we propose the new concept of
quantum-inspired bits in our study.
Additionally, we wish to highlight a currently prominent and cutting-edge area:
“quantum-inspired metasurfaces” [R1]. This field represents the forefront of research, where
metasurfaces operate in the classical domain yet can mimic specific quantum effects—such as
utilizing non-separable states to mimic quantum entanglement [R2], mimicking quantum
tunneling effects [R3][R4], and constructing time crystals [R5]. These metasurfaces are not
intended for quantum information processing but aim to achieve efficient information
processing within classical systems, drawing inspiration from quantum effects.

[Introduction]
In recent years, the continuous advancement of quantum mechanics1-3 has drawn increasing
attention to the field of quantum information science. As a revolutionary discipline bridging
quantum physics and information science, quantum information science4-6 is poised to
transform scientific and technological paradigms due to its immense application potential and
advantages. Specifically, quantum communication7-10 ensures the security of information
based on the principles of quantum physics, while quantum computing11-14 offers
computational capabilities that surpass those of classical computers, driving revolutions in
materials science, chemistry, and biomedicine. Furthermore, advancements in quantum
sensing15-18 and measurement19-21 technologies have significantly enhanced the performance
of traditional sensing and measurement systems.
The allure of quantum information science has not only catalyzed the development of
quantum metasurfaces22-25 but also fostered the flourishing of quantum optics26,27.
Metasurfaces28-32 are planar artificial structures composed of subwavelength unit cells,
designed in a periodic or non-periodic arrangement. Although initial metasurfaces lacked the
ability to modify electromagnetic (EM) responses post-fabrication33,34, which limited their
practical applications, researchers have proposed the concept of reconfigurable metasurfaces
as a solution to this limitation35-38. In contrast to traditional classical metasurfaces,
quantum metasurfaces represent a significant advancement, providing a critical research platform for
generating, manipulating, and detecting non-classical EM waves. However, the stringent
conditions required for the fabrication, manipulation, and testing of quantum metasurfaces
currently pose significant challenges to their practicality.
Concurrently, the concept of digital coding metasurfaces39 has evolved into that of
information metasurfaces40-48, bridging the realms of classical physics and information
science. While the basic information processing units of information metasurfaces are based
on classical bits, which offer stability, ease of storage and transmission, and straightforward
operation, they exhibit limitations in scalability and parallel processing capabilities. In
contrast, quantum bits49-51 present unprecedented advantages in computational speed and
parallelism, enabling the resolution of complex problems that classical bits cannot tackle.
Nevertheless, quantum bits are often unstable, making storage and transmission challenging,
and they are highly sensitive to environmental disturbances, necessitating complex error
correction techniques. Consequently, implementing their advantages within classical systems
remains a formidable challenge. This underscores the need for a feasible physical platform
capable of mimicking the characteristics of quantum bits while achieving a high degree of
computational freedom in stable classical EM systems. The concept of quantum-inspired
metamaterials52,53 provides a promising avenue for addressing this challenge.
